claim: HIV's envelope (Env) protein evolves very rapidly.
source: HIV's envelope (Env) protein evolves very rapidly.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the subsequent citations and data in the manuscript.

claim: Descendants of the pandemic HIV-1 virus have evolved so rapidly that their Envs now have as little as 65% protein identity.
source: The descendants of this virus have evolved so rapidly that their Envs now have as little as 65% protein identity (Lynch et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lynch et al., 2009.

claim: Protein orthologs shared between humans and mice have diverged to a median identity of 78% over 90 million years.
source: For comparison, protein orthologs shared between humans and mice have only diverged to a median identity of 78% over 90 million years (Waterston et al., 2002; Hedges et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Waterston et al., 2002; Hedges et al., 2006.

claim: Env's rapid evolution erodes the efficacy of most neutralizing antibodies.
source: Env's rapid evolution has dire consequences for anti-HIV immunity, since it erodes the efficacy of most neutralizing antibodies (Albert et al., 1990; Wei et al., 2003; Richman et al., 2003; Burton et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Albert et al., 1990; Wei et al., 2003; Richman et al., 2003; Burton et al., 2005.

claim: The immediate evolutionary space accessible to any given Env is largely defined by the effects on viral fitness of all single amino acid mutations to Env.
source: The immediate evolutionary space accessible to any given Env is largely defined by the effects on viral fitness of all single amino acid mutations to Env.
evidence: This is a conceptual statement that frames the study's rationale.

claim: Deep mutational scanning can measure the effects of many or even all single amino acid mutations to an Env variant.
source: although it has recently become possible to use deep mutational scanning to measure the effects of many (Al-Mawsawi et al., 2014; Duenas-Decamp et al., 2016) or even all (Haddox et al., 2016) single amino acid mutations to an Env variant.
evidence: Supported by citations to Al-Mawsawi et al., 2014; Duenas-Decamp et al., 2016; Haddox et al., 2016.

claim: During protein evolution, substitutions at one site can change the effect of mutations at other sites.
source: During protein evolution, substitutions at one site can change the effect of mutations at other sites (Natarajan et al., 2013; Gong et al., 2013; Harms and Thornton, 2014; Podgornaia and Laub, 2015; Starr and Thornton, 2016; Klink and Bazykin, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Natarajan et al., 2013; Gong et al., 2013; Harms and Thornton, 2014; Podgornaia and Laub, 2015; Starr and Thornton, 2016; Klink and Bazykin, 2017.

claim: Substitutions can become entrenched via epistatic interactions with subsequent changes.
source: Such shifts can accumulate as substitutions become entrenched via epistatic interactions with subsequent changes (Starr et al., 2017; Pollock et al., 2012; Shah et al., 2015; Bazykin, 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Starr et al., 2017; Pollock et al., 2012; Shah et al., 2015; Bazykin, 2015.

claim: The magnitude of shifts in amino acid preferences is usually limited.
source: although the magnitude of these shifts is usually limited (Doud et al., 2015; Chan et al., 2017; Ashenberg et al., 2013; Risso et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Doud et al., 2015; Chan et al., 2017; Ashenberg et al., 2013; Risso et al., 2015.

claim: Epistasis among a few combinations of Env mutations has been experimentally demonstrated.
source: Indeed, epistasis among a few combinations of Env mutations has been experimentally demonstrated (da Silva et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to da Silva et al., 2010.

claim: Epistatic fitness landscapes have been computationally inferred for a variety of HIV proteins including Env.
source: and epistatic fitness landscapes have been computationally inferred for a variety of HIV proteins (Kouyos et al., 2012; Ferguson et al., 2013; Mann et al., 2014; Barton et al., 2015) including Env (Louie et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kouyos et al., 2012; Ferguson et al., 2013; Mann et al., 2014; Barton et al., 2015; Louie et al., 2018.

claim: Env forms a large heavily glycosylated heterotrimeric complex that transitions through multiple conformational states.
source: However, the only protein-wide experimental studies of how amino acid preferences shift during evolution have examined proteins that are structurally far simpler than Env, which forms a large heavily glycosylated heterotrimeric complex that transitions through multiple conformational states (Munro et al., 2014; Ozorowski et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Munro et al., 2014; Ozorowski et al., 2017.

claim: Most sites show no detectable shifts in amino acid preferences between the two Envs.
source: Most sites show no detectable shifts, but 30 sites have clearly shifted preferences.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: 30 sites have clearly shifted amino acid preferences between the two Envs.
source: Most sites show no detectable shifts, but 30 sites have clearly shifted preferences.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Shifts in amino acid preferences are only slightly enriched at sites that have substituted between the Envs.
source: Surprisingly, shifts are only slightly enriched at sites that have substituted between the Envs—and many occur at residues that do not even contact substitutions.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Many shifts in amino acid preferences occur at residues that do not even contact substitutions.
source: Surprisingly, shifts are only slightly enriched at sites that have substituted between the Envs—and many occur at residues that do not even contact substitutions.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Long-range epistasis can unpredictably shift Env's mutational tolerance during HIV evolution.
source: Therefore, long-range epistasis can unpredictably shift Env's mutational tolerance during HIV evolution, although the amino acid preferences of most sites are conserved between moderately diverged viral strains.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The amino acid preferences of most sites are conserved between moderately diverged viral strains.
source: Therefore, long-range epistasis can unpredictably shift Env's mutational tolerance during HIV evolution, although the amino acid preferences of most sites are conserved between moderately diverged viral strains.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: BG505 and BF520 are from clade A of the major (M) group of HIV-1.
source: Both BG505 and BF520 are from clade A of the major (M) group of HIV-1.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the viral strains used in the study.

claim: BG505 and BF520 are identical at 721 of the 836 pairwise-alignable protein sites (86.2% identity).
source: BG505 and BF520 are identical at 721 of the 836 pairwise-alignable protein sites (86.2% identity).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of the two Env sequences.

claim: In the ectodomain and transmembrane domains of Env, BG505 and BF520 are identical at 549 of the 616 sites (89.1% identity) that are alignable across clade A Envs.
source: In the ectodomain and transmembrane domains of Env, BG505 and BF520 are identical at 549 of the 616 sites (89.1% identity) that are alignable across clade A Envs (Figure 1—source data 1, Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of the mutagenized regions of the two Env sequences.

claim: The BG505 Env has been extensively studied from a structural standpoint.
source: The BG505 Env has been extensively studied from a structural standpoint (Julien et al., 2013; Lyumkis et al., 2013; Pancera et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2014; Sanders et al., 2015; Stewart-Jones et al., 2016; Gristick et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple structural studies.

claim: Variants of the BG505 Env are being tested as vaccine immunogens.
source: and variants of this Env are being tested as vaccine immunogens (Sanders et al., 2013, Sanders et al., 2015; de Taeye et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sanders et al., 2013, Sanders et al., 2015; de Taeye et al., 2015.

claim: The BF520 Env was isolated from an infant who developed an early broad anti-HIV antibody response.
source: The BF520 Env was isolated from an infant who developed an early broad anti-HIV antibody response (Goo et al., 2014; Simonich et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goo et al., 2014; Simonich et al., 2016.

claim: The authors excluded the signal peptide and cytoplasmic tail from mutagenesis to reduce the degree to which they simply identified mutations that affected Env expression.
source: Mutations in the signal peptide and cytoplasmic tail commonly affect Env expression level (Chakrabarti et al., 1989; Yuste et al., 2004; Li et al., 1994), so we excluded these regions with the goal of reducing the degree to which we simply identified mutations that affected Env expression.
evidence: This is a methodological decision supported by citations to Chakrabarti et al., 1989; Yuste et al., 2004; Li et al., 1994.

claim: The deep mutational scanning effectively selected for functional Envs as evidenced by strong purifying selection against stop codons.
source: The deep mutational scanning effectively selected for functional Envs as evidenced by strong purifying selection against stop codons.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of the deep sequencing data.

claim: The error-corrected frequencies of stop codons drop to 3–16% of their original values.
source: The error-corrected frequencies of stop codons drop to 3–16% of their original values (Figure 3—source data 1)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis.

claim: The error-corrected frequencies of nonsynonymous mutations drop to 43%–49% of their original values.
source: The error-corrected frequencies of nonsynonymous mutations also drop substantially (43%–49% of their original values)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis.

claim: The frequencies of synonymous mutations drop only slightly (85%–95% of their original values).
source: whereas the frequencies of synonymous mutations drop only slightly (85%–95% of their original values).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis.

claim: Nonsynonymous mutations are often deleterious.
source: These trends are consistent with the fact that nonsynonymous mutations are often deleterious
evidence: This is a general principle of molecular evolution.

claim: Synonymous mutations often have only mild effects on viral growth.
source: whereas synonymous mutations often (Zanini and Neher, 2013) have only mild effects on viral growth.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zanini and Neher, 2013.

claim: The replicates for BG505 are more correlated with each other than with replicates for BF520, and vice versa.
source: While the replicates are well correlated across all replicates for both BG505 and BF520, the replicates for BG505 are more correlated with each other than with replicates for BF520, and vice versa (Figure 3B, compare red and blue versus gray plots).
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 3B.

claim: There is a trend for highly preferred amino acids to be more strongly preferred in BG505 than BF520.
source: Note also that there is a trend for highly preferred amino acids to be more strongly preferred in BG505 than BF520 (most high-preference points in the gray plots in Figure 3B fall above the diagonal)
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 3B.

claim: There were modest differences in the stringency of selection between the deep mutational scans of BG505 and BF520.
source: Rather, there were modest differences in the stringency of selection between our deep mutational scans of BG505 and BF520 (Figure 3—source data 1 shows that purifying selection better purged stop codons in BG505).
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: ExpCM's informed by the deep mutational scanning of either BG505 or BF520 describe the natural evolution of Env vastly better than a standard codon substitution model.
source: Table 1 shows that ExpCM's informed by the deep mutational scanning of either BG505 or BF520 describe the natural evolution of Env vastly better than a standard codon substitution model.
evidence: This is a result from the phylogenetic analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: External selection (e.g. from immunity) drives Env to fix amino acid mutations faster than expected under a null model that only accounts for functional constraints on the protein.
source: indicating that external selection (e.g. from immunity) drives Env to fix amino acid mutations faster than expected under a null model that only accounts for functional constraints on the protein.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the omega > 1 result from the ExpCM analysis.

claim: The experimental selections are more lax than natural selection on HIV.
source: a finding that makes sense, since the stop-codon analysis in the previous section suggests that the experimental selections are more lax than natural selection on HIV.
evidence: This is an inference from the stringency parameter and stop codon analysis.

claim: Residues T257, D368, E370, W427, and D457 are important for Env binding to CD4.
source: For instance, residues T257, D368, E370, W427, and D457 are important for Env binding to CD4 (Olshevsky et al., 1990)
evidence: Supported by citation to Olshevsky et al., 1990.

claim: All CD4-binding residues (T257, D368, E370, W427, and D457) are highly preferred in the deep mutational scanning.
source: and all these amino acids are highly preferred in our deep mutational scanning (Figure 4 and Figure 5).
evidence: This is a comparison of the experimental results to prior knowledge.

claim: Env has 10 disulfide bonds linking specific sites.
evidence: This is a structural fact about Env.

claim: Most of Env's disulfide bonds are important for function.
source: most of which are important for function (van Anken et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to van Anken et al., 2008.

claim: The cysteines at disulfide bond sites are highly preferred in the deep mutational scanning.
source: and the cysteines at these sites are highly preferred in our deep mutational scanning.
evidence: This is a comparison of the experimental results to prior knowledge.

claim: Env has five variable loops that mostly evolve under weak constraint in nature.
source: For instance, Env has five variable loops that mostly evolve under weak constraint in nature (Starcich et al., 1986; Zolla-Pazner and Cardozo, 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Starcich et al., 1986; Zolla-Pazner and Cardozo, 2010.

claim: Most sites in Env's variable loops are mutationally tolerant in the deep mutational scanning.
source: and most sites in these loops are mutationally tolerant in our deep mutational scanning (see sites indicated by gray overlay bars in Figure 4 and Figure 5, such as 132 to 195).
evidence: This is a comparison of the experimental results to prior knowledge.

claim: The experiments do a reasonable job of authentically measuring functional selection on Env.
source: the concordance of our findings with the above mutational studies, and the fact that our data improve phylogenetic models of Env's natural evolution, suggest that our experiments do a reasonable job of authentically measuring functional selection on Env.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: The identified sites evolving faster or slower than expected are similar regardless of whether the BG505 or BF520 experiments are used.
source: The identified sites are similar regardless of whether we use the experiments with BG505 or BF520 (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 9C.

claim: The amino acid preferences of most sites are similar in both BG505 and BF520 Envs.
source: The reason the results are similar for both experimental datasets is that (as discussed above) the amino acid preferences of most sites are similar in both Envs
evidence: This is a conclusion from the comparison of the two datasets.

claim: Either the BG505 or BF520 dataset provides a reasonable approximation of the site-specific functional constraints across the clade A Envs.
source: suggesting that either dataset provides a reasonable approximation of the site-specific functional constraints across the clade A Envs in Figure 1.
evidence: This is an inference from the similarity of results between the two datasets.

claim: Most of the sites of faster-than-expected evolution are on the surface of Env.
source: Most of the sites of faster-than-expected evolution are on the surface of Env (Figure 9A, B and Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the structural analysis in Figure 9.

claim: Env's escape from autologous neutralizing antibodies often involves amino acid substitutions in surface-exposed regions.
source: Env's escape from autologous neutralizing antibodies often involves amino acid substitutions in surface-exposed regions (Moore et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Moore et al., 2009.

claim: Sites where substitutions are antibody-driven will evolve faster in nature than expected from the experiments.
source: Since our deep mutational scanning did not impose antibody pressure, sites where substitutions are antibody-driven will evolve faster in nature than expected from the experiments.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental design and the observation of faster-than-expected evolution.

claim: Immune selection offers a plausible explanation for the sites that evolve slower than expected.
source: Interestingly, immune selection also offers a plausible explanation for the sites that evolve slower than expected.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Env employs strategies to reduce its susceptibility to antibodies including shielding immunogenic regions with glycans.
source: These strategies include shielding immunogenic regions with glycans (Wei et al., 2003; Stewart-Jones et al., 2016; Gristick et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Wei et al., 2003; Stewart-Jones et al., 2016; Gristick et al., 2016.

claim: Env employs strategies to reduce its susceptibility to antibodies including hiding immunogenic regions by adopting a closed protein conformation.
source: or hiding them by adopting a closed protein conformation (Kwong et al., 2002; Guttman et al., 2015; Ozorowski et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kwong et al., 2002; Guttman et al., 2015; Ozorowski et al., 2017.

claim: Sites that contribute to general immune-evasion strategies will be under a constraint in nature that is not present in the experiments.
source: Sites that contribute to such general immune-evasion strategies will be under a constraint in nature that is not present in our experiments—and indeed, such sites evolve more slowly than expected from our experiments.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental design and the observation of slower-than-expected evolution.

claim: Of the 21 N-linked glycosylation sites shared between BG505 and BF520, only four are under strong selection to maintain the glycan in the experiments.
source: Of the 21 N-linked glycosylation sites shared between BG505 and BF520, only four are under strong selection to maintain the glycan in our experiments—despite the fact that most are conserved in nature (Figure 9C and Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Most N-linked glycosylation sites are conserved in nature.
source: despite the fact that most are conserved in nature (Figure 9C and Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the natural sequence data.

claim: Glycans are selected primarily for their role in immune evasion.
source: This finding concords with prior literature suggesting that these glycans are selected primarily for their role in immune evasion (Pugach et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2013; Rathore et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pugach et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2013; Rathore et al., 2017.

claim: A network of sites that help regulate Env's transition between open and closed conformations evolve slower in nature than expected from the experiments.
source: Similarly, a network of sites that help regulate Env's transition between open and closed conformations that have different antibody susceptibilities (Figure 9D) also evolve slower in nature than expected from our experiments.
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The amino acid preference maps are generally consistent with prior knowledge about sites that are important for protein properties such as receptor binding or disulfide-mediated stability.
source: These amino acid preference maps are generally consistent with prior knowledge about sites that are important for protein properties such as receptor binding or disulfide-mediated stability.
evidence: This is a summary of the validation of the experimental results.

claim: Closely homologous proteins have similar structures.
source: Fortunately for the utility of structural biology, it soon became apparent that closely homologous proteins have similar structures (Chothia and Lesk, 1986; Sander and Schneider, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chothia and Lesk, 1986; Sander and Schneider, 1991.

claim: SOSIP trimer structures from diverse Env strains remain highly similar in most respects.
source: This rough generalizability of protein structures holds even for a protein as conformationally complex as Env—for although there are many examples of mutations that alter aspects of Env's conformation and dynamics (Kwong et al., 2000; White et al., 2010; Almond et al., 2010; Davenport et al., 2013), SOSIP trimer structures from diverse Env strains remain highly similar in most respects (Julien et al., 2015; Pugach et al., 2015; Stewart-Jones et al., 2016; Verkerke et al., 2016; Gristick et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Amino acid preference maps of Env have a useful level of conservation for many purposes.
source: Our results show that amino acid preference maps of Env also have a useful level of conservation for many purposes.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: From a qualitative perspective, the amino acid preferences look mostly similar between BG505 and BF520.
source: From a qualitative perspective, the amino acid preferences look mostly similar between BG505 and BF520
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The complete maps of mutational effects will be useful for future sequence-structure-function studies.
source: Indeed, we anticipate that the complete maps of mutational effects in Figure 4 and Figure 5 will be useful for future sequence-structure-function studies.
evidence: This is a prediction about the utility of the study's results.

claim: A subset of sites change markedly in which mutations they tolerate.
source: Consistent with studies of other proteins (Natarajan et al., 2013; Harms and Thornton, 2014; Doud et al., 2015; Starr et al., 2017), we find a subset of sites that change markedly in which mutations they tolerate.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, consistent with prior work.

claim: Some shifted sites simply accommodate more amino acids in the more stable BG505 Env.
source: Some shifted sites simply accommodate more amino acids in the more stable BG505 Env—a type of shift that has been well-documented for other proteins (Wang et al., 2002; Bloom et al., 2006; Gong et al., 2013; Kumar et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, consistent with prior work.

claim: There is no strong trend for shifts to be enhanced at sites that differ between BG505 and BF520.
source: But interestingly, there is no strong trend for shifts to be enhanced at sites that differ between BG505 and BF520.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: A prior protein-wide comparison of amino acid preferences across homologs of influenza nucleoprotein found a significant enrichment of shifts at sites of substitutions.
source: Indeed, a prior protein-wide comparison of amino acid preferences across homologs of influenza nucleoprotein found a significant enrichment of shifts at sites of substitutions (Doud et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Doud et al., 2015.

claim: There is some entrenchment of differences between BG505 and BF520.
source: But although there is some entrenchment of differences between BG505 and BF520, this is not the major factor behind the shifts in amino acid preferences
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: The majority of sites that have shifted between BG505 and BF520 actually have the same wild-type amino acid in both Envs.
source: the majority of sites that have shifted between BG505 and BF520 actually have the same wild-type amino acid in both Envs even though the preferences have shifted.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Env's exceptional conformational complexity might explain why shifts are not enriched at sites of substitutions.
source: This rather surprising result might be due to Env's exceptional conformational complexity—mutations can cause long-range alterations in Env's conformation (Kwong et al., 2000; White et al., 2010; Almond et al., 2010; Davenport et al., 2013), so it seems plausible that they might also shift mutational tolerance at distant sites.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: The large-scale datasets of mutational effects in multiple viral strains should be useful for efforts to computationally parameterize 'fitness landscapes' of Env.
source: Regardless of the exact mechanism, our large-scale datasets of mutational effects in multiple viral strains should be useful for efforts to computationally parameterize 'fitness landscapes' of Env (Kouyos et al., 2012; Ferguson et al., 2013; Mann et al., 2014; Barton et al., 2015; Louie et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a prediction about the utility of the study's results, with citations to relevant work.

claim: BG505 and BF520 Envs were isolated from HIV-infected infants shortly after mother-to-child transmission.
source: We therefore selected Envs from two transmitted-founder viruses, BG505.W6M.C2.T332N and BF520.W14M.C2 (hereafter referred to as BG505 and BF520), that were isolated from HIV-infected infants shortly after mother-to-child transmission (Nduati et al., 2000; Wu et al., 2006; Goo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nduati et al., 2000; Wu et al., 2006; Goo et al., 2014.

claim: The T332N variant of BG505 Env has a common glycosylation site that is targeted by many anti-HIV antibodies.
source: We used the T332N variant of BG505 Env because it has a common glycosylation site that is targeted by many anti-HIV antibodies (Sanders et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sanders et al., 2013.

claim: The authors have previously created comprehensive codon-mutant libraries of the BF520 Env and used them to map HIV antibody escape.
source: We have previously created comprehensive codon-mutant libraries of the BF520 Env and used them to map HIV antibody escape (Dingens et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Dingens et al., 2017.

claim: The BF520 libraries have not been characterized with respect to how mutations affect viral growth prior to this study.
source: but these BF520 libraries have not been characterized with respect to how mutations affect viral growth.
evidence: This is a statement about what was not done in prior work.

claim: The authors made several modifications to the earlier deep mutational scanning strategy to apply it to transmitted-founder Envs and to reduce experimental noise.
source: Here, we made several modifications to this earlier strategy to apply it to transmitted-founder Envs and to reduce the experimental noise.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of the study.

claim: The authors used SupT1.CCR5 cells instead of SupT1 cells to support growth of viruses with transmitted-founder, CCR5-tropic Envs.
source: instead of SupT1 cells, we used SupT1.CCR5 cells (SupT1 cells that express CCR5 in addition to CXCR4 [Boyd et al., 2015]) to support growth of viruses with transmitted-founder, CCR5-tropic Envs
evidence: This describes a methodological modification, with citation to Boyd et al., 2015.

claim: The authors performed a short high-MOI infection instead of a full second passage to enable recovery of env genes from infectious virions without bottlenecking.
source: and rather than performing a full second passage we just did a short high-MOI infection to enable recovery of env genes from infectious virions without bottlenecking (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes a methodological modification.

claim: The deep mutational scanning was performed in full biological triplicate for both BG505 and BF520.
source: We performed this deep mutational scanning in full biological triplicate for both BG505 and BF520 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The libraries encompassed all codon mutations to all sites in Env except for the signal peptide and cytoplasmic tail.
source: Our libraries encompassed all codon mutations to all sites in Env except for the signal peptide and cytoplasmic tail.
evidence: This describes the scope of the mutagenesis.

claim: The libraries were mutagenized at 670 sites in BG505 and 662 sites in BF520.
source: Our libraries were mutagenized at 670 sites in BG505 and 662 sites in BF520
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the mutagenesis.

claim: There is no strong trend for shifts to be enhanced at sites that differ between BG505 and BF520.
source: But surprisingly, for both the closed and open conformations, the typical magnitude of shifts is not significantly larger at sites that have substituted, or at sites that contact sites that have experienced substitutions (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis.

claim: There is a borderline trend for the significantly shifted sites to be more likely to have substituted between BG505 and BF520.
source: There is a borderline trend for the significantly shifted sites to be more likely to have substituted between BG505 and BF520 (Figure 7—source data 1)
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: Most shifted sites have not substituted (only 8 of the 30 shifted sites differ in amino acid identity between the two Envs).
source: but most shifted sites have not substituted (only 8 of the 30 shifted sites differ in amino acid identity between the two Envs).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: The lack of strong enrichment in shifts at substituted sites contrasts with previous protein-wide experimental and simulation-based studies.
source: The lack of strong enrichment in shifts at substituted sites contrasts with previous protein-wide experimental (Doud et al., 2015) and simulation-based (Pollock et al., 2012; Shah et al., 2015) studies of shifting amino acid preferences, which found that shifts were dramatically more pronounced at sites of substitutions.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current study's findings to prior work.

claim: Env's conformational complexity and dynamics may increase the opportunities for long-range epistasis.
source: The fact that Env is extremely complex and conformationally dynamic (Munro et al., 2014; Ozorowski et al., 2017) may increase the opportunities for long-range epistasis to enable substitutions at one site to shift the amino acid preferences of distant sites.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: Many of the shifted sites cluster within regions of Env that are highly conformationally dynamic.
source: Indeed, many of the shifted sites cluster within regions of Env that are highly conformationally dynamic.
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis.

claim: One cluster of shifted sites is at the trimer apex where two of Env's variable loops pack against one another and against an adjacent protomer.
source: One cluster is at the trimer apex where two of Env's variable loops pack against one another and against an adjacent protomer.
evidence: This is a description of a structural feature.

claim: The V2 region of BF520 SOSIP trimer is more accessible to deuterium exchange than the BG505 SOSIP trimer.
source: Strikingly, this cluster of shifted sites may reflect previously observed differences in the conformational dynamics of this regions between these two Envs; the V2 region of BF520 SOSIP trimer is more accessible to deuterium exchange than the BG505 SOSIP trimer (Verkerke et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Verkerke et al., 2016.

claim: Another cluster of shifted sites is near a network of hydrophobic amino acids that has been proposed to help transmit the large-scale conformational change that takes place upon CD4 binding.
source: The other cluster of shifted sites is near a network of hydrophobic amino acids that has been proposed to help transmit the large-scale conformational change that takes place upon CD4 binding (Ozorowski et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ozorowski et al., 2017.

claim: Nearly half of the shifted sites (13 out of 30) are in two clusters in conformationally dynamic regions.
source: In total, these two clusters consist of nearly half of the shifted sites (13 out of 30).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the structural analysis.

claim: Sites that are conformationally dynamic tend to be sites that show shifts in their amino acid preferences during evolution.
source: It is difficult to discern exactly how these interactions might occur, but there is certainly a trend for sites that are conformationally dynamic to also be sites that show shifts in their amino acid preferences during evolution.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the structural analysis.

claim: In the absence of entrenchment, mutating a site in BG505 to its identity in BF520 should have the opposite effect of mutating the site in BF520 to its identity in BG505.
source: In the absence of entrenchment, mutating a site in BG505 to its identity in BF520 should have the opposite effect of mutating the site in BF520 to its identity in BG505.
evidence: This is a conceptual explanation of entrenchment.

claim: The average effect of mutations that convert BG505 to BF520 or vice versa is deleterious.
source: As expected under entrenchment, the average effect of these mutations is deleterious
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: There are a substantial number of sites where the mutational flips between BG505 and BF520 are not deleterious.
source: although there are a substantial number of sites where the mutational flips are not deleterious.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Even unfavorable inter-Env mutational flips are generally more favorable than random amino acid mutations.
source: This comparison shows that even unfavorable inter-Env mutational flips are generally more favorable than random amino acid mutations.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Entrenchment occurs for some but not all substitutions that distinguish BG505 and BF520.
